title: Why is `ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent(key, expensiveLambda)` a hot-path trap under high TPS — the mapping function runs WHILE holding the bin's lock, so a slow lambda serializes every thread hashing to that bin into a thundering herd (CPU burned on park/unpark context switching, not computation) — and how do you fix it (decouple read from compute: a `Caffeine` `AsyncLoadingCache` with `refreshAfterWrite` returns the STALE value instantly to all readers while ONE background thread recomputes, so zero readers block)?
shortTitle: Why is ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent a hot-path trap under high TPS?

s1_definition.profdef: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent is a hot-path trap when the mapping function is slow because that function runs while the map holds the internal lock on the bin (the bucket) that the key hashes to. ConcurrentHashMap locks per bin rather than globally, which is efficient for fast operations, but computeIfAbsent deliberately holds the bin lock for the entire duration of the mapping function to guarantee the value is computed exactly once. So if the lambda does something slow — a database call, a heavy computation, an external request — every other thread whose key hashes to the same bin blocks on that lock, serializing them. Under high transactions per second this becomes a thundering herd where dozens of threads pile up waiting on one lock, and the CPU is consumed not by useful work but by parking and unparking threads and the resulting context switching. The fix is to decouple the read from the compute: use a cache like Caffeine's AsyncLoadingCache with refreshAfterWrite, which returns the current (possibly slightly stale) value to all readers instantly and non-blockingly, while exactly one background thread performs the recompute, so no reader ever blocks on the computation.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine a shared ledger cabinet with many drawers, and a rule that says "if the figure you need is not in its drawer, compute it and file it, and keep the drawer locked while you compute so nobody files a duplicate." That rule is fine when computing takes a second, but if computing the figure means phoning a slow external office for two minutes, then every other clerk who needs anything from that same drawer stands frozen at the cabinet for two minutes, unable to do anything — and a crowd builds up, shuffling their feet and wasting energy doing nothing (the context-switch churn). The fix is to change the rule: anyone who looks in the drawer immediately gets the figure that is currently filed, even if it is a few minutes old, and meanwhile just one designated clerk quietly phones the slow office in the back to refresh it. Now nobody ever freezes at the cabinet — they grab the current figure and move on, and the refresh happens out of everyone's way.

sections.s2_technical:
To understand the trap you first need to understand how ConcurrentHashMap achieves concurrency. It does not use a single global lock; instead it divides its table into bins (buckets), and an update to a key locks only the bin that key hashes to, so operations on keys in different bins proceed in parallel. This fine-grained locking is why ConcurrentHashMap scales well for fast reads and writes. The key word is fast: the design assumes the work done while holding a bin lock is tiny, like comparing keys and swapping a reference.

computeIfAbsent breaks that assumption when the mapping function is slow. Its contract is that the mapping function is invoked atomically — the value is computed at most once even under concurrency, and other threads touching the same key will see the completed value, not a half-built one. To provide that guarantee, the implementation holds the bin's lock for the entire execution of the mapping function. So when you write computeIfAbsent with a lambda that calls a database or does an expensive computation, you are holding the bin lock for the whole slow operation. This is explicitly warned against in the JavaDoc, which says the computation should be short and simple and must not attempt to update any other mappings of the map.

Under low traffic this is invisible, but under high transactions per second it becomes a serialization point and then a thundering herd. Suppose the key is a hot one — a popular account, a shared rate, a configuration value — that many requests need. The first thread to miss enters the mapping function and takes the bin lock. Every subsequent thread that hashes to the same bin (which includes every thread wanting that same hot key, plus any thread wanting any other key in that bin) now blocks waiting for that lock. Because the lambda is slow, the lock is held for a long time, so the waiting threads pile up. The operating system parks these blocked threads and must later unpark them, and this parking, unparking, and context switching consumes CPU and scheduler time. The paradox is that the machine looks busy — high CPU — but almost none of that CPU is doing useful work; it is spent on the overhead of managing a crowd of threads all waiting on one lock. Throughput collapses precisely when load is highest.

There is a second, subtler problem specific to computeIfAbsent on ConcurrentHashMap: if the slow lambda itself tries to access the same map (for example to look up or update another key), it can deadlock or, in some JDK versions, throw, because it is called while the bin lock is held. This reinforces that the mapping function must be trivial.

The correct fix is to decouple the read from the compute so that reading the cached value never waits on computing a fresh one. A purpose-built cache does this; Caffeine's AsyncLoadingCache combined with refreshAfterWrite is the canonical solution. AsyncLoadingCache returns a CompletableFuture for each key, and with refreshAfterWrite the behavior on a read of a value older than the refresh duration is to return the current value immediately — not block — and schedule the reload to happen asynchronously on a background executor. Crucially, Caffeine ensures only one reload is in flight per key, so even though many threads read the stale value, only one background computation runs. So all readers get a fast, non-blocking answer (the current value), and exactly one thread does the expensive work off the hot path. Compared to computeIfAbsent, no reader ever holds or waits on a lock around the slow computation.

A small code contrast makes it concrete. The trap looks like `map.computeIfAbsent(accountId, id -> expensiveLoad(id))`, where expensiveLoad blocks the bin lock. The fix builds a cache like Caffeine newBuilder with refreshAfterWrite of some seconds and an async loader, then reads with `cache.get(accountId)` which returns a future that completes with the current value immediately and triggers at most one background refresh when the value is stale. For the initial population (the very first miss where there is no value yet), Caffeine handles concurrent first-loads with single-flight too, so even the cold start does not stampede.

A senior nuance is choosing the right staleness behavior. refreshAfterWrite returns a stale value while refreshing, which is ideal when a slightly old value is acceptable (a displayed figure, a cached rate) and you never want readers to block. If you instead need readers to wait for a value only on the very first load but never again, you combine it appropriately, and if you cannot tolerate any staleness you may need a different design, but the whole point is that blocking all readers on a slow synchronous compute is almost never the right answer on a hot path. Another nuance is that even for a plain in-memory memoization without external I/O, if the computation is non-trivial you should prefer a proper cache with single-flight semantics over computeIfAbsent precisely because computeIfAbsent's lock-holding behavior does not scale. A final nuance is observability: the symptom of this trap in production is high CPU with low useful throughput and threads stacked in a parked state on a ConcurrentHashMap bin, and recognizing that signature quickly points you at a slow lambda inside computeIfAbsent.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India caches an expensive computed exchange rate used on a hot payment path, and the first implementation used computeIfAbsent.

Problem 1 — The rate for a popular currency pair was loaded with computeIfAbsent and an expensive lambda that called a slow pricing service. Under high transactions per second, every payment thread needing that rate blocked on the bin lock while the one computing thread waited on the slow service. This is the lock-held-during-slow-lambda trap.

Problem 2 — Dozens of threads piled up on that single bin lock, the CPU spiked from park/unpark churn, and throughput collapsed even though almost no useful work was being done. This is the thundering herd burning CPU on context switching.

Problem 3 — The team replaced it with a Caffeine AsyncLoadingCache with refreshAfterWrite, so every payment thread gets the current rate instantly and non-blockingly, while exactly one background thread refreshes the rate from the pricing service. This is the decouple-read-from-compute fix.

We will model the broken computeIfAbsent path where many threads serialize on a slow compute, and the fixed async-cache path where readers never block and only one background refresh runs, logging the contrast in blocking and refresh counts.

The code will have a `PricingService` (slow source), a `BrokenRateCache` using computeIfAbsent with a slow lambda, a `FixedRateCache` emulating an AsyncLoadingCache with refreshAfterWrite and single-flight refresh, and a demo running many concurrent reads against each.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a slow pricing service with two hundred milliseconds of latency and sixteen concurrent reader threads all wanting the same hot currency rate.

Step 1 — In the broken version, the sixteen threads start simultaneously and all call computeIfAbsent for the same key, which hashes to one bin. The first thread enters the mapping function and takes that bin's lock, then begins the slow two-hundred-millisecond pricing call while still holding the lock.

Step 2 — The other fifteen threads reach computeIfAbsent for the same bin and block on the held lock. They are parked by the operating system, and the demo records how many are waiting at once. No useful work happens on these threads; they are simply queued behind the one slow computation.

Step 3 — The threads are released one after another as the lock becomes available, so their total wall-clock time stacks up far beyond a single compute, reflecting the serialization. The CPU during this period is consumed by parking and unparking rather than computing, which is the thundering-herd signature.

Step 4 — In the fixed version, the cache is warmed with one initial load so a current value exists. Then the sixteen threads read concurrently. Each read returns the current value immediately without taking any lock around the slow compute, so all sixteen finish almost instantly.

Step 5 — Because the value is older than the refresh interval, the first reader to notice flips the single-flight flag and submits exactly one background refresh to the dedicated executor, while every other reader simply returns the current value. So all readers were non-blocking and only one background recompute ran, in stark contrast to the broken version where the slow compute was on the critical path of blocked threads.

```
2026-10-24 17:40:15 [INFO] === BROKEN: computeIfAbsent — threads serialize on the bin lock ===
2026-10-24 17:40:15 [WARNING] 16 readers took 213ms (serialized); compute calls=1, max blocked waiters=16
2026-10-24 17:40:15 [INFO] === FIXED: AsyncLoadingCache + refreshAfterWrite — zero readers block ===
2026-10-24 17:40:15 [INFO] 16 readers took 1ms (all instant); background refreshes=1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  BROKEN: computeIfAbsent(key, slowLambda)
  16 readers → same key → same BIN
    thread-1 ─▶ take bin lock ─▶ [slow 200ms compute] ─▶ release
    thread-2..16 ─▶ BLOCK on bin lock ─▶ parked (context-switch churn)
    → serialized; high CPU, ~0 useful work; throughput collapses under load

  FIXED: AsyncLoadingCache + refreshAfterWrite
  16 readers → cache.get(key)
    ├─ all 16 ─▶ return CURRENT value instantly (non-blocking)
    └─ value stale? ─▶ single-flight CAS ─▶ ONE background thread recomputes
                                              (off the hot path)
    → zero readers block; exactly one recompute regardless of reader count
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent becomes a hot-path trap when the mapping function is slow, and to explain why I start with how the map achieves concurrency: it locks per bin rather than globally, so operations on keys in different bins run in parallel, and that design assumes the work done while holding a bin lock is tiny. computeIfAbsent breaks that assumption because, to guarantee the value is computed exactly once, it holds the bin's lock for the entire duration of the mapping function. So if my lambda calls a database or does an expensive computation, I am holding the bin lock for that whole slow operation, which the JavaDoc explicitly warns against.

Under high transactions per second this turns into a thundering herd. For a hot key that many requests need, the first thread to miss takes the bin lock and runs the slow lambda, and every other thread hashing to that same bin — which includes everyone wanting that hot key — blocks on the lock and gets parked by the operating system. As load rises, dozens of threads pile up waiting, and the CPU is consumed by parking, unparking, and context switching rather than by useful work. The machine looks busy with high CPU, but almost none of it is productive, and throughput collapses exactly when load is highest. There is also a subtler hazard: if the slow lambda tries to touch the same map, it can deadlock, because it runs while the bin lock is held.

The fix is to decouple the read from the compute so reading the cached value never waits on computing a fresh one, and the canonical solution is Caffeine's AsyncLoadingCache combined with refreshAfterWrite. With that, a read of a value older than the refresh interval returns the current value immediately and non-blockingly and schedules the reload to run on a background executor, and Caffeine ensures only one reload is in flight per key. So all readers get a fast answer — the current, possibly slightly stale value — while exactly one thread does the expensive work off the hot path, and no reader ever holds or waits on a lock around the slow computation.

In my banking work this was a real production incident: an expensive computed exchange rate on a hot payment path was loaded with computeIfAbsent and a slow pricing call, and under peak load the payment threads serialized on the one bin lock, the CPU spiked from park/unpark churn, and throughput collapsed even though the actual pricing work was trivial in volume. We replaced it with a Caffeine AsyncLoadingCache and refreshAfterWrite, after which every payment thread got the current rate instantly and a single background thread refreshed it, and the collapse disappeared.

The nuances I always add are that refreshAfterWrite deliberately trades a little staleness for never blocking, which is the right trade for a displayed or cached figure but not for an authoritative value; that even for pure in-memory memoization you should prefer a proper cache with single-flight semantics over computeIfAbsent whenever the computation is non-trivial, because computeIfAbsent's lock-holding does not scale; and that the production signature of this trap is high CPU with low useful throughput and threads parked on a ConcurrentHashMap bin, which is exactly what points me at a slow lambda inside computeIfAbsent.
